When his family managed to get through him by phone, he shouted one word, water, before the line went dead. They never heard from him again. Three years have passed since the dam's destruction. The site remains under Russian occupation, and no one has been held accountable for the death of hundreds of civilians, including Anatoly. During this Council's 62nd session, Anatoly's granddaughter, Anastasia, spoke about her family's quest for justice. To support them and six other families who lost relatives in this attack, Legal Action Worldwide and Truth Hounds filed a complaint to the Human Rights Committee in June arguing that Russia violated their right to life. We urge the Human Rights Committee to address this complaint and to prioritize other outstanding submissions related to Russia's war of aggression, some registered over four years ago. States should also support independent investigations into the dam's destruction and champion accountability for the victims. Mr. Vice President, what can this Council do to ensure that those responsible are held to account And that the families of the victim can receive answers and obtain recognition. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the representative of Plan International intervention by video.

My name is Sonia and I'm a participant in Plan International's Champions of Change program, which helps young people understand their rights, challenge gender inequality and take an active role in their communities. I'd like to share my experience as a young girl living through the war and raise some of the issues that matter to young people in Ukraine today. I was born in little Kharkiv, but when the war started, I moved to Kyiv. Adapting to a new school was difficult, but having real contact with my peers was very important to me. My friends in Kharkiv still study online and miss face-to-face communication. For young education is not only about lessons. We need socialization and safe spaces where we can feel connected and supported. Accessibility is another issue I notice in everyday life. Because of the war, more people in Ukraine are living with disabilities, yet many public spaces are still not accessible. Through the Champions of Change program, I have started thinking more about gender equality and youth challenges. Young people need early education on health, relationships, consent, and boundaries, information that can be limited during the war. While we teach girls self-protection, we must also teach boys about respect, equality, and responsibility. So, my message to decision-makers is simple: ensure that children affected by the war can not only learn but also socialize and feel safe. Make Ukraine's recovery inclusive and accessible, and give young people, especially girls, a meaningful role in decisions. A decisions about our future should not be made without us.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the representative of ACT Alliance, intervention by video.

Excellencies, I speak for the ACT Ukraine Forum and the wider ACT Alliance, a global coalition of over 160 faith-based organizations. Right now in Ukraine, humanitarian missions are under fire. Medical hubs and aid convoys are destroyed, and civilians experience the harsh reality of war. As local faith actors, we are rooted within communities, and we are often on the front line, serving as first responders. We stay because these are our communities, and this is where we live. The deepest wounds of war are often invisible. They shatter the mind and they break the human spirit. That is why our network in Ukraine prioritizes mental health and the protection of civilians, reaching out to those who need it most. We urge the international community. ensure that support for those traumatized by war is fully resourced, so that they can be a part of building a better tomorrow. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the representative of Human Rights Now.

Human Rights Now remains deeply concerned about the human rights and humanitarian crisis caused by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. According to UN reports, civilian casualties from January to August this year have already exceeded the total for all of last year. Furthermore, a September report recorded 1,004 cases of sexual violence from the start of the invasion to the end of July this year, with 89% attributed to Russian authorities. Many occurred in occupied areas of Ukraine and included gang rape, genital mutilation, and electric shocks. The sexual violence must stop immediately, regardless of the perpetrator. However, the Russian Federation bears a particularly heavy responsibility to take concrete actions, given the high number of violations by its officials. Perversely, Russia has instead implemented laws granting broad immunity for crimes, including sexual violence, committed during military service. Reports also show that Russia is conducting large-scale, systematic transnational repression against Ukrainian critics by a variety of means in multiple countries. We call on the Russian government to immediately end the conflict in Ukraine and on the international community to strengthen support for accountability initiatives for all human rights violations and war crimes by the Russian government against Ukrainians. We also urge states to refuse any cooperation with Russia's transnational repression and to enhance efforts to protect victims.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the representative of Human Rights Research League. Intervention by video.

Thank you. Behind every statistic about war is a child. Since Russia's full-scale invasion, Ukrainian children have been killed, injured, displaced, separated from their families, and deprived of safety. The latest report documents 1,004 cases of conflict-related sexual violence. Among those attributed to Russian authorities were girls and boys, and the youngest were just 4 years old. But the consequences of war do not end when the violence stops. Our survey of 138 parents and guardians of war-affected children found that 54% reported increased irritability or emotional instability, 43% high anxiety, and 47% signs of premature adulthood. The greatest concerns were their children's future, the direct impact of war, and emotional well-being. These children included those who lost parents, children of missing persons, POWs, and fallen defenders, as well as children who experienced deportation, displacement, or occupation. Territorial concession cannot substitute for human security, as no child is safe living under the Russian occupation, as it exposes children to coercion, indoctrination, militarization, separation, and other grave violations. We must stop Russia's aggression, punish responsible for the war crimes, return Ukraine children to Ukraine, as every child returned is a life restored. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the representative of Human Rights House Foundation.

President, the latest United Nations monitoring of the human rights situation in Crimea continues to show severe restrictions on fundamental rights, including freedom of expression, access to Ukrainian education, and protection from forced conscription. Our partners in Human Rights House Crimea are documenting a further escalation in the use of Russia's criminal justice system against residents. New analysis by Crimean Process shows a dramatic rise in prosecutions for so-called high treason since the full-scale invasion. Such trials are held behind closed doors and can result in extraordinarily severe sentences. In one recent case, a court hearing lasted just 90 minutes, resulted in a 16-year prison sentence. At the same time, the space for documenting these violations is disappearing. Following its designation as a foreign agent, Crimean Solidarity, which for a decade documented political persecution and supported prisoners and their families, was forced to cease its activities. We also remain deeply concerned for Crimean citizen journalist Iryna Danilovych, whose rights and conditions of detention continue to deteriorate, including reports of arbitrary searches and other violations. Vice President, we ask the High Commissioner: How can the United Nations strengthen or assist monitoring of closed and politically motivated trials in the occupied parts of Ukraine? I thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the representative of Juventum, intervention by video.

Mr. High Commissioner, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Juventum is honored to participate. In the fifth year of the war in Ukraine, the aggressiveness and the cruelty in attacking civilians are escalating. Unmanned weapons and landmines are being used. The use of nuclear and autonomous weapons is suggested. Civilian infrastructure providing essential services, including energy, is also targeted. International humanitarian law and human rights are violated, and war crimes are committed. We call for an immediate ceasefire through peace negotiations, respecting the UN Charter and other international laws. Please let us not forget that the nuclear facilities in this conflict area are in danger. The Chernobyl plant, which is known for the world's biggest nuclear accident was once occupied. Europe's largest Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant is under occupation, and its safety is threatened. IAEA keeps warning about the precarious situation of the nuclear facilities in Ukraine. Even without the war, Nuclear power is not worth risking life, health and the environment. Its low electricity output efficiency means huge additional warming of the planet. The discussion of this war must be globally responsible too. Thank you very much for your attention.

Thank you.

This was the last speaker on my list. And I will give the floor to Mr. Volker Turk for his concluding remarks.

Well, thank you, Mr. Vice President. And I am fully conscious that year after year, session after session, we report back to you on the horrible human rights situation in Ukraine. And I have to say, if we, and as I just, as we just reported, including through the public reports that we provide, we are confronted with an intensification of hostilities, with an escalation with a terrible plight, a terrible impact on civilians and on civilian infrastructure, and in civilian infrastructure that goes well beyond the energy sector. I cannot even fathom what Ukrainians feel these days with the onset of winter and of the winter season, and what they would expect. And I have to say it is really important when we have these discussions that we just imagine the plight of the victims. When we issue reports to all those who question them, I can only say that we do it on the basis of a very strict methodology that we apply, tried and tested, that we have explained ad nauseam to various delegations. So what we put forward is what we not only can provide in terms of evidence, but also in terms of the testimonies verified by us multiple times, and that's what we can put forward as evidence and as facts. And when it comes to the practice of conflict-related sexual violence, I have to say the evidence that we have collected points to conflict-related sexual violence that is widespread in nature. Across the incidents assessed, we are seeing patterns and commonalities that do suggest practices that beyond an established accumulation of individual cases. I think that's important to remember. And we see the adoption of laws in Russia that exempt service persons from criminal liability for crimes, including from sexual violence, which is obviously very concerning because we need exactly the opposite. When we have such allegations and such reports, we need urgent investigations and we need independent access to those people who are affected by that. It's also clear that survivors of conflict-related sexual violence need to be very much at the center of justice and accountability efforts, which requires safe reporting for them, I mean, trauma-informed investigations, confidential, timely, accessible, survivor-centered medical, psychosocial support, and legal services. We need the preservation of evidence, and we need to make sure that the international community insists with the Russian Federation that they investigate these crimes. And that's extremely important. On the civilian detainees and the prisoners of war, There should be absolute zero tolerance for torture, inhuman, degrading treatment. There is indeed, as part of confidence building, we need exchanges, and I welcome the exchanges that have taken place for prisoners of war, but there should be an all-out effort to exchange an all for all, to have an all for all exchange of prisoners of war, and to release civilian detainees that are arbitrarily detained. We should also call, continue to call on the Russian Federation to provide independent, impartial monitors, including my office, which I have asked several times for access to places of internment, to share information about the whereabouts and the fate of prisoners of war, including third country nationals and civilian detainees, to facilitate communication with their families and to establish mixed medical commissions as required under the Geneva Conventions. You've asked about the attacks on energy infrastructure, some of you. Well, it's not just energy infrastructure, as I mentioned, it goes beyond energy infrastructure as we speak. I mean, this could be one of the first confidence-building measures that one could immediately agree upon to stop attacking civilian infrastructure. It's not only required by international humanitarian law and international human rights law, it's also required by pure empathy for the other, for the human being. And it's also clear that in the process of rebuilding any of this, we need to ensure that there is a particular focus on vulnerable groups and people with special needs. We also need to ensure continued emphasis on access to the occupied territory, especially through public diplomatic engagement with the authorities of the Russian Federation. We should have access, we used to have access, we need access again, and that includes all places where POWs are held and civilians are held. And it is also absolutely critical that any future peace agreement places strong emphasis on the rights of people and the international legal framework that is provided for this purpose for people who are living currently in occupied territory, and that includes those detained by the Russian Federation. I will be I will continue to be open to any engagement with everyone who wants to engage with us and to ensure that we exercise our work in the pursuit of human rights, in the pursuit of peace, in line with the Charter and international law. Thank you, Mr. Vice President.

Thank you.

This brings us to the end of this interactive dialogue, and I wish to thank the High Commissioner for his participation. We will now take a short break before holding the enhanced interactive dialogue on the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Excellencies, distinguished participants, we will now begin the enhanced interactive dialogue on the High Commissioner's report on the situation of human rights in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, pursuant to Council Resolution 60/35. It is my honor to welcome Ms. Awa Dabo, Deputy High Commissioner, for Human Rights, who will present the High Commissioner's report. I also welcome to the podium His Excellency Mr. Samuel Mdemba Kabuya Tanda, Minister of Human Rights of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Mr. Jean-Claude Katende, National President of the African Association for Defense of Human Rights. The list of speakers will close in 15 minutes. I now give the floor to the Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights for her presentation. You have the floor, madam.

Mr. Vice President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, good afternoon. I would like to begin by offering my deepest condolences for the tragic helicopter crash that killed 17 people on Friday, 25th September in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Among the victims were the President of the High Military Court, Joseph Mutombo Katelayi, and the Auditor General of the Congolese Armed Forces, Lucien Rene Likulia. Both had worked towards accountability for gross human rights violations, including conflict-related sexual violence. Their loss is deeply felt, and I hope the momentum to advance this important cause can be maintained. Mr. Vice President, the people of the DRC are caught in a painful convergence of crises: the Ebola virus outbreak, decades of violent conflict and mass displacement, and competition over the exploitation of the country's natural resources. The Ebola virus outbreak, the largest and deadliest ever in DRC, continues to take a heavy toll, particularly in Ituri and North Kivu provinces. According to the latest figures, the outbreak has surpassed 8,000 confirmed cases, with more than 3,900 deaths. The outbreak has further strained health systems, weakened by decades of conflict and chronic underinvestment in public services. Funding shortfalls and persistent insecurity are hampering efforts to reach communities, detect cases, and trace contacts. Longstanding grievances about public institutions and international aid groups are also affecting the health response. Those trying to contain the diseases are themselves under attack, often fueled by misinformation about the virus. As of 11 September 2026, Our office documented at least 36 death threats, attacks against healthcare personnel and facilities, and interference with burials. The recent killing of a politician after a radio appearance to raise awareness about Ebola is a sign of how deadly fear and misinformation can become. Sustained engagement with communities grounded in transparency, equity, and respect for everyone's rights is essential to rebuilding trust. Mr. Vice President, The security situation in DRC remains extremely alarming. Between 1 January and 15 September 2026, our government documented approximately 4,400 human rights violations and abuses in North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri provinces, affecting some 9,500 victims. Violations include unlawful killings, restrictions on civic freedoms and violations, and abuses of international humanitarian law. The prevalence of conflict-related sexual violence is particularly worrying. Between 1 June 2025 and 31 May 2026, our office documented at least 1,080 victims of conflict-related sexual violence across the country, primarily women and children. This is nearly three documented victims of sexual violence per day, and the true figures are likely higher. Armed groups are reportedly responsible for 42% of the victims. Women and girls were attacked while going about their daily activities, in their homes, while working in their fields, in the bush, and along the roads. These crimes must end. Survivors need support and protection, and those responsible need to be held accountable. Accountability is possible even in war. With support from our office, judicial authorities have conducted five joint investigative missions and held eight mobile court hearings on allegations of conflict-related sexual violence. This led to the conviction of 161 members of the Congolese armed forces and 30 members of armed groups, amongst others. The authorities protected the identity of 620 women victims and witnesses during the trial. The authorities need to build on these steps, and our Office is ready to assist. In Ituri Province and in parts of North Kivu, attacks against civilians by the Allied Democratic Forces continue, including abductions and sexual violence. Between 1 January and 15 September 2026, our Office attributed 319 human rights abuses to the ADF, affecting more than 1,500 victims. In North Kivu and South Kivu, violent clashes have intensified since mid-September between the M23, supported by the Rwandan Defence Forces, and the Congolese Armed Forces, supported by Wazalendo groups. This escalation comes despite commitments made under the Doha and Washington peace processes and the African Union-led efforts. According to the latest figures available, more than 6.1 million people are internally displaced across the country. Mr. Vice President, the guns must fall silent urgently. People need to see an improvement in their daily lives, to be able to go to school, to work, and to meet their families in safety. All parties to the conflict need to ensure full respect for international human rights law and humanitarian law. We reiterate our call on the Rwandan government to withdraw its troops from the DRC and end its support to the AFC M23. We also continue to urge that ongoing peace processes be anchored in human rights. This means ensuring accountability for grave crimes. It also means integrating the legitimate aspirations of victims for truth, justice, and reparations, and guarantees that the crimes will not happen again. Our office has shared a set of human rights-based confidence building measures with the parties to the conflict and with the mediators under the Doha, Washington, and AU-led peace processes. They are practical, time-bound, and verifiable actions to protect civilians and to create conditions for peace to take root. They need to complement and strengthen existing initiatives, and our office is ready to support. For a chance at peace, people need to be able to speak freely and to participate and hold those in power to account, yet across the country, Journalists, human rights defenders and political opponents continue to face arrests, intimidation and other attacks. We welcome the announcement by the authorities that they intend to organize a national dialogue. This needs to be an inclusive process that addresses the underlying drivers of conflict, protects civic space and helps to build sustainable peace. To that end, the authorities need to ensure the meaningful participation of women, youth, civil society, human rights defenders, journalists, and affected communities. There needs to be a shared national vision for a society and an economy that works for everyone, with revenues channeled into better health care, quality education, and social protection for all. Investing in human rights is essential for both peace and sustainable development. We call on member states to continue to support human rights in the DRC. Mr. Vice President, there is a profound paradox between the DRC's immense mineral wealth and the widespread poverty of its people. Ruthless competition over natural resources and economic interests, both within and outside the country, continue to fuel the conflict in the east. Our office is ready to support mandatory, human rights impact assessments for major natural resource projects and investments. The country's resources should benefit the people of the DRC, not be exploited by self-serving foreign and domestic interests. This requires accountability, governance reforms, tackling corruption, and stronger institutions. Thank you.

Thank you.

I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Samuel Mthembu-Kabuya-Tanda for his presentation.

Distinguished Vice President, Madam Deputy High Commissioner, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, on behalf of His Excellency, President of the Republic President Tshilungo and Her Excellency the Prime Minister, Head of Government, Ms. Tshiluka, and the people of my country, I thank the Deputy High Commissioner for the oral update. I thank the Human Rights Council for the constant focus on the human rights situation in my country. The resolution 60/35 on technical assistance and capacity building in human rights in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is a crucial framework for cooperation with the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and all of the international human rights mechanisms. Vice President, the human rights situation in my country remains marked by mass violence carried out by Rwanda and its lackeys, the AFC M23, led by Paul Kagame, former president of the DRC, Kabila, and Mr. Kony Nganga, who formed the hierarchy, rapes, torture, enforced disappearances, enforced displacement, exploitation of children for economic and military purposes, and mass killings of entire communities. resultant of genocide are increasingly widespread. The data cited in the report illustrate this clearly. On 2nd August 2026, we commemorated the genocost, and at that time, the occupying forces arrested 37 young people in Menova calling for the withdrawal of Rwandan troops. 17 girls were raped. Amnesty International's report of 21st September 2026 documented the summary executions, acts of torture, ill treatment, arbitrary detentions, forced labor, forced recruitment, pillaging, and trafficking of gold and cotton towards Rwanda in the mining areas of Rubaya in North Kivu and Lemera in South Kivu. The DRC condemns these egregious violations of human rights and IHL and calls on Rwanda to withdraw its troops from our territory in line with the regional resolutions and several United Nations resolutions, in particular the Human Rights Council resolutions. Furthermore, the government is pursuing its efforts to promote and protect human rights on several levels, combating impunity, consolidating the implementation of forensic medicine and its integration in criminal law, transitional justice, the guiding principles and voluntary principles for the protection of human rights in the extraction sector. And an ongoing re-dynamization of the provincial human rights services, the training of public officials and law enforcement in human rights and international humanitarian law. Here, I would wish to emphasize that my government does not have a policy of restricting political liberties or violating human rights. Isolated cases documented are investigated and sentenced. There are 560 sentences handed down, reflected in the report of the High Commissioner. The last complaint for human rights violations at the last political demonstrations are now being investigated by the judiciary. Vice President, and technical assistance, my country wishes to ensure that this is coordinated and oriented towards tangible needs and to its internal institutions, for example, support to the process for implementing transitional justice. capacity building in forensic investigations, identification of victims, exhumations, preservation of evidence, and management of human remains. And I call on our partners to support the training of our new generation of forensic doctors and specialists. This corresponds to one of the precise commitments under the resolution 6035. Vice President, in conclusion, my country calls on states, United Nations agencies, international financial institutions, and bilateral and multilateral partners to mobilize financial humanitarian, technical, logistic resources for the effective implementation of resolution 60/35. My country is determined to continue its unflagging efforts and strengthen the rule of law. I am convinced that cooperation based on capacity building at the national level will make it possible to transform the commitments contained in resolution 60/35 into tangible results for the benefit of the Congolese people. Finally, I call on the High Commissioner to provide the independent commission of inquiry in the DRC under resolution S/37/2019 with the necessary resources in order that it may carry out its mission, which must be completed in March 2027. I thank you.
Thank you, Your Excellency. I now give the floor to Mr. Jean-Claude Katende for his presentation.

Thank you, Mr. President. President, ladies and gentlemen, the African Association for Human Rights, ADOH-CG, would like to draw your attention to the worrying situation of human rights in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the following terms: the Democratic Republic of the Congo is a country at war. This is an unjust war imposed upon it by Rwanda, a war that we denounce, given the numerous human rights violations which are committed. In this context of war, the human rights situation is experienced in a different fashion, whether people reside in the occupied territories or in those that are not occupied. In the occupied territories, our organization is concerned by the reprisals against civilians, particularly against women and children, committed by all forces involved in the armed conflict. in violation of the civil peace agreement between Rwanda and the DRC. In this territory, journalists and human rights defenders are regularly harassed by the M23 and AFC forces. Some have lost their lives, while others were forced to flee into other cities of the countries or even abroad. We also remain concerned by the increasing numbers of victims of sexual violence and the resurgence of human rights violations directly linked to the illegal exploitation of natural resources. In the non-occupied territories, our organization remains concerned by the restriction of civic space, marked by regular violations of the freedom of expression, the right to assembly in Kinshasa. Two demonstrations of the opposition on the 12th of June and the 15th of September 2026 were dispersed with many people injured during the process. In other areas of the country, such demonstrations were outright prohibited. We are also concerned by the arrests and arbitrary detention operated by the National Intelligence Agency and the Council of Cyber Defense. In a country already divided by war, the current law under discussion in the parliament on referendum on changes to the constitution is a source of great concern given the socio-political upheavals that such an initiative could give rise to in the country, Mr. President. In this context, we call on member states to strengthen their support to civil society and to the protection of human rights defenders. We would also ask your council to require of the government of the DRC to open the civic space. Thank you.

Thank you.

The list of speakers is now closed. According to established practice, we will start by hearing the delegation of the country concerned. I understand that the delegation of Rwanda does not wish to take the floor at this stage. I now invite interested delegations to ask questions to the presenters and to make comments on their statements. Please be reminded that the speaking time is one minute and 30 seconds for all speakers. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Sweden on behalf of a group of countries.

Mr. Vice President, Thank you, Deputy High Commissioner, for the report, which we welcome and support. I deliver this statement on behalf of the Nordic-Baltic countries. The human rights situation in eastern DRC remains deeply worrying. We are particularly concerned by reports of unlawful killings, persistent conflict-related sexual violence, recruitment and use of children, shrinking civic space, and continued attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure. We strongly condemn all violations and abuses of human rights and violations of international humanitarian law committed by all parties to the conflict. We support ongoing regional and international mediation efforts to secure a sustainable ceasefire and advancing a peaceful resolution to the conflict. All parties must uphold and deliver on their commitments. immediately de-escalate the situation, ensure the protection of civilians, facilitate safe and unhindered humanitarian access, and fully comply with international law. We stress that efforts must continue to ensure that all those involved in the murders of UN experts Saida Khattalane and Michael Sharp are held to account. Deputy High Commissioner, How can the root causes of violations and abuses of IHL and human rights law in eastern DRC most effectively be addressed? Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the Distinguished Representative of the European Union.

Thank you, Mr. President. The European Union thanks the Deputy High Commissioner for the presentation of her report. We firmly condemn all human rights violations and abuses committed by armed groups as well as by state actors. We are particularly concerned by summary executions, abductions, recruitment and the use of children, hate speech, as well as conflict-related sexual violence. In this context, we welcome the mandate of the Commission of Independent Inquiry. The EU reiterates its appeal to the M23, supported by Rwanda, to put an end to its offensive and to the forces of defence of Rwanda to withdraw from DRC. We are also preoccupied by the shrinking of civic space, arbitrary detentions aimed at political actors and others, as well as the most serious violations. The European Union welcomes the decision of the prosecutor of the ICC to reactivate inquiries on alleged crimes committed. And we reiterate that those who are responsible for the deaths of the UN representatives must be brought to justice. There must be an immediate moratorium on the death penalty. Madam Deputy, High Commissioner, what priority measures can the international community take to best support and protect civic space and human rights defenders in the current context? Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Rwanda.

Mr. Vice President, the Council needs a comprehensive assessment of the drivers of human rights violations in the DRC. A conflict spanning more than 30 years cannot be reduced to selective allegations against Rwanda. This item should focus on DRC's capacity, institutional weaknesses, and protection challenges. Resolution S/13/35 identifies the FDLR, Codeco, Azarengo, and ADF as groups of concern, but the report before this Council omits the continued activities of the DRC-backed FDLR and the DRC's recruitment of foreign mercenaries. The report acknowledges that FRDC is supported by Wazalendo, but omits the government's responsibility to protect civilians and ensure accountability. Hate speech persists with Tutsi communities among its primary targets. Protecting people from identity-based persecution is a human rights obligation, not preferential treatment. Lastly, Major General Ekenge has been reinstated as spokesperson of the FRDC. despite his discriminatory remarks documented in this report. What message does this send about the DRC government's stated commitment to accountability and ending impunity during this session? Item 10 should assist the DRC in confronting its human rights challenges, not become a politicized item to externalize its responsibility towards its own citizens. I thank you, Mr. Vice President.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Togo.

Mr. President, the delegation of Togo thanks the High Commissioner for his report and remains concerned by the persistent armed violence in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. of which the women and children are the main victims, in particular through sexual violence and forced displacement and other serious violations of their rights. Togo condemns all human rights violations, as well as violations of international humanitarian law, whoever the perpetrators might be. The protection of civilians, fighting impunity, and victims' access to justice must remain at the core of any response to this crisis. We welcome the efforts of the DRC government against impunity and in favor of transitional justice. Mr. President, my delegation remains convinced that dialogue and the upholding of commitments must remain at the core of the peace process. In this context, Togo reiterates its support to the process of peace of Doha and Washington, as well as the mediation efforts of the African Union And we encourage all parties to continue their commitment to fully implement them in order to achieve a lasting peace and strengthen the protection of civilian population. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Gabon.

Mr. Vice President, the delegation of Gabon welcomes the holding of this enhanced dialogue and thanks the Deputy High Commissioner for the clarity of her report. We welcome the tangible efforts achieved by the DRC in promoting and protecting human rights. which has taken the form, amongst others, of budget options to earmark funds for access to justice, education, health care and social protection. Moreover, we welcome the RDC's efforts to take positive action in terms of transitional justice, as well as in fighting impunity and restoring peace and the state authority. Mr. President, the DRC remains confronted with security challenges and human rights challenges, in particular in the areas affected by the conflict. We are concerned by all human rights violations and violations of international humanitarian law against civilians, attacks against civilians, sexual violence and forced displacement, abductions, as well as Grave violations committed against children are a serious source of concern. We encourage the government to continue its efforts to promote social cohesion, and we call on the international community to support efforts to achieve a lasting peace in the east of the DRC, in particular through technical assistance which is coordinated. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation.

Mr. Vice President, the situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo leads to serious concern amidst continued armed conflict between the government and rebel groups. As a result, we have seen the further deterioration of the humanitarian situation, accompanied by mass human rights violations and violations of international humanitarian law, large-scale displacement of the population, and an increase in the number of forced migrants. The number of refugees has exceeded 1 million, and of IDPs, 10 million. Despite international efforts, there are continued clashes between the government and the March 23 movement. This has led to a serious deterioration of the humanitarian situation, as well as the outbreaks of infectious diseases. We believe there is no military solution. Parties must return to a political and diplomatic settlement of the conflict in line with UN Security Council Resolution 2773. We count on the activation of regional peacekeeping efforts through the mediation of the African Union, in line with the principle of African solutions to African problems. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

Mr. President. The UK thanks the High Commissioner for his report and remains deeply concerned by the grave human rights situation, particularly in eastern DRC. We are alarmed by continuing reports of unlawful killings, conflict-related sexual violence, the recruitment and use of children, arbitrary detention and attacks against schools, healthcare facilities and civilian infrastructure. The findings of the UN's investigations underline the gravity of the situation facing civilians in eastern DRC. We are particularly concerned by the impact of the conflict on women and children, the continued displacement of millions of people and the obstacles this creates for the delivery of humanitarian assistance. We are also concerned by the continued transmissions of Ebola, which is exacerbating vulnerabilities among conflict-affected populations and placing strain on already overstretched health services. The UK reiterates its support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the DRC and calls on all parties to comply with international human rights law and international humanitarian law. Those responsible for violations and abuses must be held accountable. What further action is needed from the international community to strengthen civilian protection, support the response to the Ebola outbreak and ensure accountability for human rights abuses and violations? Thank you.

This trend must continue, particularly through credible investigations, which are impartial, and strengthening of national institutions for the protection of human rights and for justice. In parallel, transitional justice initiatives are making progress in a number of provinces. There have been consultations allowing victims to be heard and to contribute to the national reflections on justice, truth, reparations, and guarantees of non-recurrence. Finally, responsible governance of natural resources remains strategic for the country's future. The mineral wealth of the DRC must contribute to peace, sustainable development, respect for human rights. Impact assessments on human rights carried out by the joint office are an essential tool in prevention and in building trust between businesses, communities and the authorities. This progress illustrates the essential conviction that investing in human rights is investing in peace. Vice-President. The progress is real, but it remains fragile. The violence continues. Humanitarian needs remain enormous. The Ebola outbreak accentuates the need of conflict-affected populations. Cholera in certain areas is an additional pressure on communities and essential services, which are severely stretched. We must maintain our collective efforts, and I call on the authorities to continue and step up their efforts to protect civilians and civic space and to strengthen the rule of law. It is also essential for the perpetrators of violations to be brought to account. We must maintain our political, technical and financial support. a sustainable commitment to peace in the DRC. Human rights must remain at the heart of all peace initiatives and those for security and development. In conclusion, a simple message: human rights are not a consequence of peace, they are one of the preconditions for peace. Peace that does not protect civilians cannot last. Peace that that leaves victims without justice will remain fragile. Peace, which does not respect dignity and the rights of all, will remain incomplete. In the DRC, despite the breadth of the challenges, progress is possible. Our collective responsibility now is to transform that into a measurable change in the lives of people. More security, more justice, more protection. more hope. Victims and communities must not be alone in bearing the weight of this crisis. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, thank you for these very rich and constructive contributions. They reflect the continued attention you devote to the human rights situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and to the work of OHCHR in the country. In response to the questions asked, on civic space and human rights defenders, The OHCHR stresses the importance of prevention through stronger legal and institutional frameworks, capacity building for law enforcement officials, inclusive dialogue amongst authorities, opposition actors and civil society, and accountability to prevent violations and combat impunity. On the root causes of violations in the eastern DRC, we would like to emphasize the need to place human rights at the center of peace and governance efforts. including tackling impunity, strengthening the rule of law, addressing the illegal exploitation of natural resources, protecting civic space, and promoting inclusive governance, accountability, community participation, and victims' access to justice remain essential for sustainable peace. Mr. Vice-President, allow me to conclude with these three brief observations. Firstly, Any sustainable solution to the conflict in the eastern DRC must address its economic dimensions, including competition among state, private actors, and other actors over the country's vast natural resources, many of which are critical to the global energy transition. Secondly, Human rights remain central to addressing the root causes of the conflict and building lasting peace. This is the rationale behind OHCHR. We encourage all stakeholders engaged in the peace process to take ownership of these measures, and we stand ready to support their implementation. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honour to present the country reports of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the Secretary-General on Cambodia and Yemen.
